newsitem.title: FRANCE: France's Leotard cautions government on NATO.
newsitem.headline: France's Leotard cautions government on NATO.

text.p: French former defence minister Francois Leotard cautioned the government on Thursday against moving closer to NATO if it did not win concessions from Washington on reform of the Alliance.

Leotard, president of the UDF, junior partner in the centre-right ruling coalition, played down remarks by German Defence Minister Volker Ruehe that Paris had for the first time "signed a document in which NATO's nuclear defence is seen as the decisive element and the British and French nuclear systems back this up".
Ruehe was referring to a joint strategy document signed with Germany, which the French Left has denounced as sacrificing national defence sovereignty to the United States and NATO.
"There is a move in France, launched several years ago, towards a rapprochement with certain NATO structures," Leotard told RTL radio.
"But France has always been a member of the Alliance and the German minister notes that for several years now there is in fact a move to get closer...with the proviso that NATO changes," he added.

Ruehe's remarks sparked an incident in the French parliament on Wednesday, with Socialists saying Ruehe's statement upheld their view that Paris had for the first time recognised NATO's preeminence in nuclear deterrence.
Leotard said France must engineer the NATO reform which "aims to ensure that certain countries like France can use NATO means and yet still run operations of their own."
"I want today's discussions to succeed. If that is not the case, that will mean we went down the wrong road and that we weren't able to obtain what we are demanding from the Americans.

"I don't want us to go further without obtaining from the Americans guarantees on a certain number of issues -- on (southern) command, on procedures, and on how Europeans can exist as themselves inside NATO," Leotard said.

France has demanded that the United States, which provides the commander of all NATO forces in Europe based in Belgium, turn over command of southern forces to a European officer to give the allies a more active role in the post-Cold War era.

French Foreign Minister Herve de Charette has said the government was faithfully pursuing a Franco-German defence rapprochement begun by its predecessors, notably the late Socialist president Francois Mitterrand.
President Jacques Chirac and Chancellor Helmut Kohl approved the Joint Franco-German Security and Defence Concept on December 9 in Nuremberg.
Calling the two countries' security interests inseparable, it says their first commitment is to defend NATO and urges a dialogue on the role of nuclear deterrence in European defence.

Ruehe told ARD television that Germany did not aim to become a co-partner in a separate French nuclear force but rather wanted to see France's atomic weapons treated as a European part of the NATO arsenal.
"NATO...means integrated defence," he said. "We are now building up with France a European identity within NATO."
